items.title: Beyond procedural technicalities: The scope of amendment under Order VI Rule 17 CPC
items.summary: Pleadings set out a case of the parties to the suit and determine the issues to be considered by the Court. During the course of the hearing of the suit, the parties may find it necessary to amend their pleadings to incorporate additional facts, clarify existing averments, or seek further relief. Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) empowers courts to permit amendments to pleadings if such amendments are necessary for determining the real questions in controversy between the parties. The said provision seeks to balance two important considerations, i.e., ensuring that a dispute is decided completely and avoiding belated amendments that may delay proceedings or cause prejudice to the opposite party. The Supreme Court’s decision in Haramani Sahoo and Others v. Lalita Nayak and Others reiterates these principles and explains how courts should approach amendment applications filed after commencement of trial. Statutory position under Order VI Rule 17 CPC Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC permits either party to alter or amend its pleadings at any stage of the proceedings, on such terms as may be just, where the amendment is necessary for determining the real questions in controversy. However, the proviso to the said provision incorporates restrictions on filing applications seeking amendments. As per the said proviso, no application for amendment shall be allowed once the trial has commenced unless the Court is satisfied that despite due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before commencement of trial. The Supreme Court in Revajeetu Builders & Developers v. Narayanaswamy & Sons held that an application for amendment of pleadings must be considered judiciously, keeping in view whether the proposed amendment is necessary for the proper and effective adjudication of the dispute and whether it would cause prejudice or injustice to the opposite party. The Court identified relevant considerations, including the bona fides of the application, the possibility of avoiding multiple proceedings, whether the amendment fundamentally changes the nature and character of the case, and whether the amended claim would be barred by limitation. The judgment clarifies that the power under Order VI Rule 17 of CPC is discretionary and must be exercised with care, and that amendments should not be permitted merely as a matter of course. items.title: Punjab & Haryana High Court quashes Centre’s complaint against Amazon over sale of toys without ISI mark
items.summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court recently quashed a complaint filed by the Union government against Amazon over storage of toys lacking the ISI mark, the quality certification mark issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards [Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. and another v Union of India] Justice NS Shekhawat said that the registration of the proceedings against the intermediary had led to miscarriage of justice as Amazon is only a marketplace E-commerce entity, which had merely acted as a third-party facilitator for buyers and sellers. The Court also ruled that Amazon as an intermediary is protected from liability under the Information Technology Act. It further noted that the government authorities had failed to array the sellers, who had stored their goods at Amazon's Fulfillment Centre, as accused in the case. "Even otherwise, under the provisions of the Toys (Quality Control) Order, 2020, the liability under the Act to ensure the compliance of various provisions of the BIS Act is upon the person who manufactures, imports, distributes, sells, hires, leases, stores or exhibits for sale any goods," the Court held. Justice NS Shekhawat Amazon moved the High Court in 2023 after a Ludhiana court issued summons to the company and its directors on a complaint filed under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act. The complaint alleged that Central government officials had conducted a raid at the premises of Amazon and collected various toys, which were stored by third-party sellers for sale without ISI marks. The government said that Amazon had stored the toys for sale and had exhibited them for sale without an ISI mark in violation of the law. Challenging the complaint, Amazon said vague allegations had been levelled against its directors without even identifying them. The company also argued that it is only an e-commerce marketplace which allows third-party sellers to list their products for sale to customers. The Court was also told that Amazon provides storage facilities to the sellers. Amazon is not involved in manufacture, import, distribution, retail sale or lease of any of the products listed on its online marketplace by third-party sellers, it was argued. Finding sufficient force in Amazon's submissions, the Court quashed the complaint and chargesheet filed against it. However, it clarified that the government would be at liberty to ascertain the identity of those who were selling the products in violation of the law. Senior Advocate Randeep S Rai with Advocat

items.title: Supreme Court declines to entertain plea to reduce minimum age to contest elections
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Saturday refused to entertain a petition seeking a reduction in the minimum age required to contest Parliamentary and State legislature elections [ Nalla Suresh Reddy vs Union of India ]. A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh expressed that it was not appropriate for the Supreme Court to intervene in the matter, prompting the petitioner to withdraw the plea. Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Aparesh Kumar Singh During the hearing, the petitioner's counsel told the Bench that the plea raised a "vital issue" concerning the disparity between the voting age and the minimum age for a person to contest elections. He pointed out that the minimum age to contest elections continues to stand at 25 years for the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, and 30 years for the Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils. On the other hand, the 61st Constitutional Amendment had lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 years. The petitioner called for a similar reduction in the minimum age for a person to contest elections as well. However, the top court was not inclined to interfere. "This is not an appropriate petition," it said. Sensing the Court's reluctance, the petitioner's counsel then sought a limited direction to the concerned authorities to decide on a pending representation submitted by the petitioner. The Bench observed that the petitioner can approach the relevant High Court for such a direction. "For that, you can go to the High Court under Article 226," it said. The counsel then sought permission to withdraw the petition. Allowing the request, the Bench ordered the matter "dismissed as withdrawn." Articles 84 and 173 of the Constitution of India prescribe the minimum age qualifications for membership of Parliament and State Legislatures, respectively, mandating a threshold of 25 years for the lower houses and 30 years for the upper houses. Any alteration to these age criteria requires a constitutional amendment by Parliament. items.title: CLAT: Fairness first
items.summary: The difficulty of an entrance examination is the examiner’s prerogative; its fairness is the candidate’s right. CLAT may be as demanding as the Consortium of National Law Universities considers appropriate. It cannot afford uncertainty about correct answers, doubt about the security of its paper, or preventable opportunities for cheating. Warnings from the official mocks The Consortium conducted two official CLAT 2027 mocks in November 2026. The first was exceptionally demanding. Difficulty itself was not the problem: in several questions, however, the officially preferred choice appeared less defensible than an alternative. The second mock exposed a more fundamental defect. An independent question-by-question review of its 120 questions found approximately 106 in which two options were defensible, with another borderline item. This is a documented analytical assessment, not a judicial or Consortium finding, and the count is open to independent scrutiny. In a Legal Reasoning question on certiorari, two choices both said in substance that a court should not reassess facts merely because it prefers another conclusion. In Logical Reasoning, alternatives describing overcrowded transport causing unreliable journeys conveyed the same result. A candidate cannot be fairly penalised for choosing one accurate paraphrase over another. With negative marking, sound reasoning can be penalised while guessing is rewarded. There were arithmetic errors too. Question 113’s key chose ₹62,000, although 150 workers earning an average of ₹400 must earn ₹60,000. Question 120’s figures produce savings of ₹12,724, a figure absent from all four options. This is not sophisticated difficulty; it is a failure of checking. The Consortium’s mock instructions invited candidates to choose the “most accurate and comprehensive” answer where options appeared partly correct. That rule is legitimate when one option is demonstrably superior. It does not rescue choices that are effectively synonymous. Mock defects foreshadow standards candidates may encounter. The problem did not begin this year CLAT 2021 demonstrated that even a lengthy, demanding paper can attract praise for its design and administration. Subsequent editions revived concerns about ambiguous keys, the structure of General Knowledge and question booklet sets that appeared different without being meaningfully different. items.title: Judges do not deserve praise for merely doing their duty: Jharkhand High Court Justice MS Sonak at farewell
items.summary: Judges do not deserve praise for merely doing their duty and should be willing to accept criticism, Jharkhand High Court Chief Justice Mahesh Sharadchandra Sonak said on Friday. Justice Sonak was speaking at an event held to mark his retirement from judicial service. He was elevated as an Additional Judge of the Bombay High Court in June 2013 and served there for nearly 13 years before taking over as Chief Justice of the Jharkhand High Court in January 2026. In his farewell address, he expressed his discomfort with the practice of praising judges for performing their judicial duties. "I am not very comfortable with the general idea of praising the judges for doing their judicial duties. No one deserves praise for doing what he or she ought to do. Just as Oliver Wendell Holmes once bemoaned that the trouble with most of us is that we would rather be ruined by praise than be saved by criticism," said Justice Sonak. Justice MS Sonak I am not very comfortable with the general idea of praising the judges for doing their judicial duties. He went on to note that judges were not infallible. "Behind every verdict is a judge wrestling with imperfection. As judges, we are human, not infallible. As the great Benjamin Cardozo felicitously said, great tides and currents which engulf the rest of the men do not turn aside in their course and pass the judges by," said Justice Sonak. He also pointed to the pressures under which courts function. "Some of our decisions can be dialogues with generations which are yet to come. It is wrong and too great an expectation to get every judgment right. Given the pressures of our dockets we mostly decide in the heat and dust of the battlefield with no leisure for calm contemplative reflection," he noted. Justice Sonak held that criticism of judicial decisions was necessary to ensure that the judiciary remained faithful to its constitutional responsibilities. He stressed that respect for the judiciary had to be earned through its commitment to the law. "The rule of law no doubt demands reverence for the judicial office but not for the individuals who occupy it. And even that institutional respect is never an entitlement but something that must be earned and preserved each day through steadfast fidelity to law immune to the passing tides or any external noise," added Justice Sonak. items.title: Buying data, inheriting liability: Cyber and data due diligence in Indian M&A
items.summary: When a company acquires a business, it acquires that business's data, along with any failure in how that data was collected, secured or shared. That exposure is no longer theoretical. IBM's 2026 study put the average cost of a data breach in India at ₹25.5 crore ( IBM India, 2026 ). From May 13, 2027, the substantive provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) will add penalties of up to ₹250 crore. My argument is that data must be diligenced as a liability, not only valued as an asset. Transactions signed today will close, or be integrated, under the new regime. Question: Why has data become a core diligence issue in Indian transactions now? Answer: Three developments have converged. First, the DPDP Act's substantive obligations, including security safeguards and breach intimation, are scheduled to take effect on May 13, 2027 ( Mondaq, Aug 2026 ), giving a target's compliance gaps a statutory price. Second, the regime reaches back into existing databases. Under Section 5(2), where consent was obtained before the Act commenced, the Data Fiduciary must issue a fresh notice as soon as reasonably practicable ( Fox Mandal ). Legacy customer data brings remediation work, not just records. Third, the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 already require specified cyber incidents to be reported within six hours and ICT logs to be retained for a rolling 180 days. A target's incident history is therefore a checkable record. Consider a consumer application whose price rests on marketing to its users. If their consents were bundled or unclear, that value may be harder to realise once the new requirements bite. The asset and the liability sit in the same database. Question: Who becomes responsible for the target's data under the DPDP Act? Answer: It depends on the deal structure. Section 8(1) makes a Data Fiduciary responsible for compliance for processing undertaken by it or on its behalf, irrespective of any agreement to the contrary . The question is who the Fiduciary is after closing. In a share acquisition, the target's historical non-compliance stays with the target, and therefore with the value of the shares. In a business transfer, the Act does not expressly say whether consents given to the seller extend to the buyer's processing. Section 17(1)(e) is narrower than often assumed. items.title: Delhi High Court bars Bajaj Finance from using AI-facial recognition cameras to profile visitors without consent
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday restrained Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Finance Securities and Bajaj Housing Finance from using artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled facial recognition cameras at its branches and authorised dealer stores to allegedly capture and profile customers and others who visited their offices/ dealerships. Justice Jasmeet Singh said that the company can continue to use the technology for Know Your Customer (KYC) verification but cannot use the tech to capture images of any and every person walking into their store, without their consent. The Court added that Bajaj cannot share the data collected through these cameras with any other entity. “For the said reasons, the respondent Nos. 2 to 4 [Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Finance Securities and Bajaj Housing Finance], their agents, employees, representatives and any persons acting on their behalf are restrained from collecting and using the information collected by way of these facial recognition cameras for purpose other than KYC. Furthermore, the respondent Nos. 2 to 4 are specifically restrained from sharing the said data with any other entity, including group entities,” the Court ordered. Justice Jasmeet Singh The Court observed that profiling customers through facial recognition matched with Aadhaar-sourced data raises a serious question of privacy. “I am of the view that the concerns of the petitioner are genuine and in this day and age, where banking frauds as well as AI-based frauds are becoming increasingly prevalent, the privacy of the petitioner is of paramount importance,” the Court said. It also referred the challenge to Bajaj Finance’s privacy policy and prayer seeking directions to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to prohibit Non-Banking Finance Companies (NBFCs) from obtaining facial biometric information through AI-enabled cameras without express and informed consent to the Division Bench that deals with public interest litigation (PILs). items.title: Is the Tribunal Reforms Act, 2026 calling for a seventh round of Madras Bar Association litigation?
items.summary: It is beyond doubt that tribunals today decide some of the most important disputes in India, covering areas such as taxation, insolvency, company law, service matters and telecommunications. In many of these disputes, the government is itself a party. This makes one question central to every round of the Madras Bar Association’s (MBA) litigation over the last 15 years: who gets to choose the people who decide these disputes and should the government have the final say in it? The Tribunal Reforms Act, 2026 , which came into force on August 25, 2026, appears to address the Supreme Court of India’s concerns. It establishes the National Tribunals Commission (NTC), as directed by the Court, and follows its directions on tenure and the number of candidates to be recommended for each post. However, it removes one safety-net that the Supreme Court has sought since 1987 and expressly required since 2010: a Supreme Court judge nominated by the Chief Justice of India (CJI) as the chairperson of the selection committees for most tribunals. This omission could lead to a seventh round of MBA litigation. Six rounds, one constant Appointments to tribunals are made on the recommendation of a search-cum-selection committee, which evaluates candidates for the posts. The composition of this committee, particularly who chairs it, has remained the central issue. In SP Sampath Kumar v. Union of India (1987), the Supreme Court observed that these committees should be headed by a sitting Supreme Court judge nominated by the CJI. In Union of India v. R Gandhi (2010), the Court made this a binding direction and gave the judicial chairperson a casting vote to resolve any tie in favour of the judicial side. In Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd (2019) , the Court struck down the 2017 Tribunal Rules framed under the Finance Act, 2017, observing that the judiciary had been reduced to “token representation”. Finally, Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2020) (MBA IV) settled the position: the CJI or his nominee must chair the selection committee and have the casting vote to ensure “judicial dominance” in the selection process. items.title: From Innovation to Incorporation: UAE Holding Companies as the Legal Infrastructure for AI Scale-Ups
items.summary: Introduction: The Convergence of AI, Law, and Global Structure Working at an AI company operating in India and looking outward to the world, I often find myself confronting a duality: the rapid evolution of AI technologies on one side and the slow moving machinery of law and compliance on the other. In this tension lies the lawyer’s strategic imperative to build structures that are legally resilient yet commercially agile. One such structure is the UAE-based holding company. Over the past few years, I have observed a pattern among growth-stage startups, especially in AI and Deep tech: they are incorporating holding companies in jurisdictions like the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), and select free zones such as DMCC. items.title: Modi's questions to corporate India expose the gaps in his economic model | Let Me Explain 182 | Pooja Prasanna
items.summary: For years, Narendra Modi and his government have sold Indians a particular economic promise: make businesses richer, encourage investment, cut corporate taxes, and the benefits will eventually reach everyone else. More jobs, better salaries, higher incomes. That's the promise of trickle-down economics. And last week, the Prime Minister had some rather pointed questions for India's corporate bosses. Where are the jobs? Why haven't salaries gone up? After all the tax cuts and incentives, what exactly have you done for the people who work for you? These are perfectly legitimate questions. But they also raise an uncomfortable political question for Modi himself. If corporate India hasn't delivered on the promise of trickle-down economics, who is accountable? The companies that received the tax breaks? Or the government that designed this economic model, and repeatedly told Indians that the benefits would follow? Across the country, young people are protesting over unemployment, recruitment delays and examination paper leaks. And the PM’s speech now shows he is cognizant of this unrest, he knows it can't be ignored. So, is Modi right about corporate India's greed? And what does his public dressing-down reveal about the economic model of his own government? Let me explain. Corporate India has questions to answer. But so does the government. items.title: ‘DMK has fallen into BJP’s trap’: Shashi Tharoor on support for Delimitation Bill
items.summary: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has criticised its former ally, the DMK party, over reports that it may support the BJP-led Union government’s proposed Delimitation Bill, saying the party risks abandoning its longstanding defence of state rights. “I think the DMK has been a very strong voice in the past for the rights of states. In fact, the DMK was in power till this year, and they won't allow the Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas to come to Tamil Nadu because they refused to allow Delhi to teach Hindi in Tamil Nadu. Now, such a party to surrender on the specious grounds that the increase is proportionate without looking at the larger agenda of the BJP behind it is, I think, an abdication of responsibility to the people in whose name they claim to speak,” the Congress MP said. Explaining the Delimitation proposal, he said, "This proportional increase argument is a very specious one. Let's say you're a Managing Director of a company and you are paying yourself Rs 2 lakh and your driver has a salary of 20,000, a proportion of 10 to 1. You announce a 50% increase for everybody. Your salary goes up to Rs 3 lakh; your driver goes up to 30,000. Are you not very much better off? Proportion is still the same, 10 to 1. But you have so much more money, so many more disposable assets, so much more you can do.” He said that the DMK has fallen into the BJP’s trap. Meanwhile, on Saturday, November 28, the DMK passed a resolution in support of the proposed Delimitation Bill in Parliament, as the draft Bill addresses most of the key demands raised by the DMK. It proposes a 50% increase in the number of Lok Sabha seats allocated to every state, delimitation of constituencies based on the latest Census, and a freeze on further delimitation until 2051. The DMK had strongly opposed the previous Constitution Amendment Bill introduced by the Union government in April 2026. The party argued that linking delimitation to population growth would disadvantage states that had invested in family planning and successfully reduced their population growth.

The southern party passed a resolution supporting the legislation at a meeting of its MPs chaired by party chief MK Stalin in Chennai on Saturday, November 28. A DMK source told TNM that the 50% uniform increase in the seats of all states, which the draft Bill proposes, has been presented as the lesser of two evils to the southern state. Such delimitation gets legal sanction from the Constitution (84th Amendment) Act of 2002. Recognising the demographic asymmetries that stemmed from differing population growth rates across different states, the 84th amendment had frozen population-based delimitation for a period of 25 years. “Keeping in view the progress of family planning programmes in different parts of the country, the government, as part of the National Population Policy strategy, recently decided to extend the current freeze on undertaking fresh delimitation up to the year 2026 as a motivational measure to enable the state government to pursue the agenda for population stabilisation,” the amendment had said. It allowed for population-based delimitation to be carried out as per the figures of the first Census after 2026. The government is said to have reminded the DMK that passing a law to carry out the exercise would require only a simple majority in Parliament. items.title: SC rejects PIL over Italian socialist leader Giacomo Filibeck’s vote fraud remarks
items.summary: Follow TNM ’ s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. The Supreme Court on Friday, November 27, refused to entertain a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) seeking action against Italian politician Giacomo Filibeck over his ‘Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod’ (Vote thief, leave the throne) slogan at the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad, asking the petitioner to approach the Union government instead. The PIL was filed by one Zahid Ali. A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh said the petitioner was free to submit a representation seeking regulations on speeches made by foreign nationals on Indian soil. “You are free to make representations. Who is stopping you?” the bench remarked, questioning the need to invoke Article 32 of the Constitution. “You can file a complaint. Why Article 32 petition?” it added. Article 32 of the Indian Constitution guarantees right to constitutional remedies and allows any person whose fundamental rights are violated to seek relief. The PIL sought intervention over Filibeck’s remarks, alleging that he had interfered in India’s domestic political affairs by criticising the government and expressing support for the Opposition. It also sought the removal of his statements from social media. The controversy had earlier triggered a political response from the Telangana BJP. On November 16, state BJP president N Ramchander Rao led a delegation to the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) in Shamshabad and submitted a complaint seeking criminal proceedings against Filibeck and the Bharat Summit organisers. Ramchander alleged that foreign delegates had used the Congress-led Telangana government’s event to interfere in India's internal affairs. He sought an investigation into possible violations of immigration laws and visa conditions. Giacomo Filibeck, secretary-general of Italy’s Party of European Socialists (PES), had raised the slogan targeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi and praised Rahul Gandhi’s campaign for clean and transparent electoral rolls. He also referred to the Opposition’s march to Ramlila Maidan in Delhi, saying citizens must stand up to defend democracy. Ramchander demanded an apology from Rahul Gandhi and Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy for applauding the remarks. He also sought Filibeck’s blacklisting, criminal action against the organisers and a probe into the backgrounds of foreign delegates. items.title: DMK to back Union government’s delimitation Bill
items.summary: The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) has decided to support the Union government’s proposed Delimitation Bill in Parliament. The party passed the resolution at a meeting of its Members of Parliament chaired by DMK president MK Stalin. The party has 22 MPs in the Lok Sabha and eight in the Rajya Sabha. The draft Bill, released by the Union government on Friday, November 27, addresses most of the key demands raised by the DMK. It proposes a 50% increase in the number of Lok Sabha seats allocated to every state, delimitation of constituencies based on the latest Census, and a freeze on further delimitation until 2051. The Bill is scheduled to be tabled in the Lok Sabha on November 30, during a special sitting of Parliament. The proposed changes come amid sustained opposition from several southern states, which have argued that delimitation based on population could penalise states that have successfully implemented family-planning measures and brought down population growth. Their concern has been that states with higher population growth could gain a greater share of parliamentary seats, reducing the relative political influence of southern states. The proposed legislation is also linked to the implementation of the 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state Legislative Assemblies. It seeks to increase the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850, with the number of elected representatives from states going up from 530 to 815. The number of seats in state Assemblies will also increase by 50%. Under the proposed arrangement, the existing proportion of Lok Sabha seats allocated to each state will be protected until 2051. The party argued that linking delimitation to population growth would disadvantage states that had invested in family planning and successfully reduced their population growth. The party's opposition was part of a wider debate over the political representation of southern states. These states have argued that they should not lose their share of parliamentary representation for achieving demographic targets encouraged by successive Union governments. Stalin had taken a strong public position against the earlier proposal and even burnt a copy of the Bill in protest. items.summary: Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has renewed his support for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led Union government’s plan to reintroduce the Delimitation Bill, citing women’s reservation. The previous Bill was defeated in Parliament after the Opposition objected to tying the women’s quota to delimitation. The CM appealed to Opposition parties not to oppose the proposal, saying that doing so would obstruct greater representation for women. Speaking to reporters in New Delhi alongside Union Minister HD Kumaraswamy, Naidu supported a proposed 50% increase in seats in every state. He argued that if delimitation were based only on population figures, southern states could be disadvantaged because they had curbed population growth more successfully. “If delimitation is undertaken based on the 1971, 2011 and 2026 Census figures, southern states could face difficulties. In the past, southern states successfully implemented population control measures. I too worked extensively on family planning in undivided Andhra Pradesh. We achieved population control through a focused campaign and succeeded in reducing the fertility rate.” “However, the situation has changed now. We are moving towards population management and providing incentives to encourage it. Under the present Union Cabinet decision, steps are being taken to increase the number of seats by 50% in every state,” he said. The DMK’s stance on delimitation softened in the months that followed, after the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) defeated it in the Assembly polls. Interestingly, it was the former DMK government led by MK Stalin that constituted a High Level Committee on Union-State Relations under retired Supreme Court judge Kurian Joseph in April 2025, to examine and review provisions of the Constitution of India, laws, and orders that bear upon Union-State relations. In a foreword to part one of the Committee’s report published in February 2026, Stalin had written that it was meant to look into the “creeping centralisation and reforms required to restore federal balance.” This committee interestingly recommended an inter-state delimitation freeze for 100 years, till 2126.
